In my remarks, I’m going to focus mainly on the national economy and its
implications for monetary policy

After more than two decades of growing at only about a one and a half
percent rate,
a.

—over the past three years, the rate has averaged an extraordinary
four and a quarter percent!

Of course, the strong productivity performance is only one of the fundamental
forces stimulating the economy’s growth at this point. Let me mention two other
important fundamentals.
1.

The Fed cut short-term interest rates from six and a half percent to
one and three-quarters percent in 2001.

And we brought the rate down to one percent with additional cuts
in November 2002 and last June.

So, over the last two years, short-term rates have been at their
lowest levels in more than forty-five years.

Real GDP advanced at a blazing rate of six percent in the second half of last year.

It was especially encouraging to see the performance of business
investment in equipment and software,
a.

This improvement in business investment has helped the beleaguered
manufacturing sector, which has begun to grow in recent months.

While output has been growing at a fast clip, I’m afraid the same can’t be said for jobs.
A.

Since the recession ended in November 2001, the overall number of jobs in the
economy has fallen, on balance.

Growth in payrolls has been in positive territory in each of the past seven
months,

Although demand for goods and services has been advancing robustly, it
has been matched or outpaced by faster productivity growth.

Of course, the recent pace of productivity growth is not sustainable in the longer
run.
1.

With productivity rates like that and a continuation of the strong demand
we’ve seen,
a.

One reason inflation has been restrained is that, until the middle of last year,
economic growth was pretty sluggish, and that led to slack in labor and product
markets—
1.

As a result, even though we’ve seen fast growth in the last few quarters,
a.

we’ll probably need to see relatively strong growth for a few more
quarters before we work off that slack.

Another factor that has restrained inflation is the acceleration in productivity
growth I’ve been talking about.

and the other is the effects of the higher price of oil on elements included
in core inflation.

In fact, recent data have shown core inflation moving up a bit relative to the
exceptionally low rates seen last year.

In fact, this is the first expansion in over forty years that began with a very
low inflation rate.

So, as long as the inflation rate has been low, upside surprises haven’t been as
much of a concern,
1.

and the FOMC has been able to “be patient” in removing its stance of
policy accommodation.

short-term rates will need to move up at some point to prevent a
rise in inflation.

A “warning” signal is that we’ve yet to see a convincing rebound in
overall employment here.
a.

And employment in the tech sector continues to slide, though at
milder rates than we saw previously.

Looking ahead, I am optimistic about the future for economic and job growth in the Bay
Area.
A.
